title: What style numbers can and cannot tell you
outcomes: States the sample (games, years, rating floor) before quoting any number about a player
Names what a given measure shows and what it does not show
Lists at least two things (era, opponents, opening choice, colour, sample size) that could explain a difference between two players
Says what extra evidence would be needed before calling a difference a habit

steps.text: **What this lesson claims, and what it does not.** It shows a few counts from our own game data for four players: Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, Levon Aronian and Hikaru Nakamura. It does **not** say who plays in which style, and it does not rank anyone. Its aim is the habit of asking, before you believe a number about a player: how many games, from when, against whom?

steps.prompt: Before any numbers: pick one word people use about a top player (for example sharp, solid, drawish). Write what you would have to count to show it, and how many games you would want.

fields.label: What I would count, and over how many games:

steps.text: **The sample.** Every number here comes from our data file: games between two players both rated 2400 or more, standard time control, duplicates removed, from The Week in Chess (issues 920 onward) and Lichess broadcasts (2020 onward). It holds *some* of each player's games, not all. For all four players it covers the years 2012 to 2026. Games: Carlsen 5,654; Nakamura 7,612; Caruana 4,963; Aronian 3,796. These counts were produced by our own script from those games; the lesson quotes them exactly and adds no other numbers.

steps.prompt: The data holds some of each player's games, not all. Name one way that could make a number about a player misleading.

fields.label: One way a partial sample misleads:

steps.text: **Evidence 1: game length.** Average game length in our data: Carlsen 47.2 moves (5,654 games), Caruana 49.7 (4,963), Aronian 46.7 (3,796), Nakamura 48.9 (7,612). This shows length only. It does not show how any game *felt*.

**Evidence 1b: queens at move 30.** Of games that reached move 30, queens were still on the board in: Carlsen 2,716 of 4,948 (54.9%); Caruana 2,924 of 4,516 (64.7%); Aronian 1,761 of 3,307 (53.3%); Nakamura 4,062 of 6,635 (61.2%). A count of queens at one moment does not show who chose to keep them.

steps.prompt: Caruana's share with queens on at move 30 is 64.7% in 4,516 games, and Aronian's is 53.3% in 3,307 games. Say what this number does NOT show, and what you would check before saying it reflects a habit.

steps.text: **A small sample.** Our file also holds Anatoly Karpov, but only 238 games from 2012 to 2022. Queens were still on at move 30 in 108 of 183 games that reached it (59.0%). That is about the same share as Nakamura's 61.2% in 6,635 games, but 183 games could move several points on a few events.

steps.prompt: How much would you trust a gap of two points between two players when one share rests on 183 games, like Karpov's? Say why.

steps.text: **Evidence 2: draws, opening choice, colour.** Share of all games drawn, in our data: Carlsen 1,671 of 5,654 (29.6%), Caruana 1,574 of 4,963 (31.7%), Aronian 1,596 of 3,796 (42.0%), Nakamura 2,226 of 7,612 (29.2%). First move with White was 1.e4 in 1,234 of Carlsen's 2,869 White games (43.0%), 1,353 of 2,507 for Caruana (54.0%), 961 of 1,919 for Aronian (50.1%) and 1,209 of 3,946 for Nakamura (30.6%).

**Evidence 3: colour changes the picture.** Carlsen won 1,769 of his 2,869 White games (61.7%) but 1,368 of 2,785 Black games (49.1%). Caruana won 1,229 of 2,507 as White (49.0%) and 976 of 2,456 as Black (39.7%). Aronian: 816 of 1,919 (42.5%) and 578 of 1,877 (30.8%). Nakamura: 2,329 of 3,946 (59.0%) and 1,806 of 3,666 (49.3%). A single win rate without colour mixes two different situations. Opponents also differ: average opponent rating in the data runs from 2,658 (Nakamura) to 2,710 (Aronian).

steps.text: **How to read a claim about a player.** Ask five things. How many games? Which years, and did the player change over them? Against whom, and in which events? Which colour? Which measure exactly, and does the word used for it (say 'sharp' or 'solid') match what was counted? A count with its sample is evidence about *that sample*; a label is an opinion until a measure defines it. For further reading, see the Library, and ask the same five questions of each source.

steps.prompt: Write one sentence about one of the four players that is true of the sample and states its limit, with the number of games. Then say how sure you are it would hold outside our data, and what could break it.
Take one label you have used about your own play, such as 'I blunder under time pressure'. Write the question, answerable from your games, that would confirm or reject it.
